documents.text:
September 9, 2026

Ms. Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C. 20426

Re:       Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC
          FERC Docket No. PF26-9-000
          Desert Southwest Expansion Project
          Draft Environmental Resource Reports 1 and 10

Dear Ms. Reese:

On March 27, 2026, in compliance with the requirements of 18 Code of Federal Regulations ("C.F.R.")
§157.21(b) 1, Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC ("Transwestern") requested that the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission ("FERC" or "Commission") begin its review of the proposed Desert Southwest
Expansion Project ("Project") using FERC's Pre-Filing Review Process ("Pre-Filing"), and FERC
assigned Docket No. PF26-9-000 to the Project. On April 3, 2026, FERC approved Transwestern's
request.

Consistent with Section 157.21(f)(10) 2 of the Commission's pre-filing procedures, Transwestern is filing
draft Environmental Resource Reports 1 and 10 for the Project. Transwestern will include final Resource
Reports 1 and 10 as part of the final Environmental Report as Exhibit F-1 to the certificate application,
which is anticipated to be filed by November 30, 2026.

On May 1, 2026, Transwestern submitted preliminary draft Resource Reports 1 and 10. Subsequently,
on June 18, 2026, Transwestern received comments ("June 18 Comments") from Commission staff on
the preliminary draft resource reports. Transwestern is including a matrix herein in Resource Report 1
(numbers 1-19) and 10 (numbers 20-31) that identifies where the information requested by FERC staff
in the June 18 Comments may be found in the draft resource reports.

This FERC filing is being submitted under the following volumes:
      •   Volume I – contains Public Information
      •   Volume II – contains Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (“CEII”)

Transwestern respectfully requests that only the information submitted as Public in Volume I be placed
on the internet as “Public Information”. In addition, Transwestern requests the CEII information
submitted in Volume II identified as “CUI/Critical Energy Infrastructure Information – Do Not
Release” be accorded special treatment pursuant to 18 CFR § 388.112.

This filing is being submitted electronically to the Commission’s eFiling website pursuant to the
Commission’s Order No. 703, Filing via the Internet Guidelines, issued on November 15, 2007, in FERC

                             1. GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

1.1     PROJECT DESCRIPTION

Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (NGA) to construct, own, and operate the
proposed Desert Southwest Expansion Project (Project). The Project is an expansion of the existing
Transwestern system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline
(mainline) and approximately 180 miles of lateral pipelines (laterals), new compressor stations (CS),
associated meter and regulator stations (M&R), and other aboveground facilities in Texas, New Mexico,
and Arizona (see Map 1.1-1).

On March 27, 2026, in compliance with the requirements of 18 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR)
§157.21(b), Transwestern requested that FERC begin its review of the Project using FERC’s Pre-Filing
Review Process (Pre-Filing Process), and FERC assigned Docket No. PF26-9-000 to the Project. On April
3, 2026, FERC approved Transwestern’s request. As part of the Pre-Filing Process, FERC, with input from
federal and state agencies and other stakeholders, analyzes environmental impacts, alternatives, and
mitigation measures prior to Transwestern’s submission of a certificate application. This allows FERC,
and other federal and state resource management agencies, to identify environmental issues associated with
the design and routing of the Project and work toward their resolution. Other agencies may participate in
the Pre-Filing Process by working with FERC to identify and resolve concerns and by attending agency
and public information meetings. The Pre-Filing Process concludes when Transwestern files its certificate
application under Section 7(c) of the NGA.

Among other requirements, FERC regulations require that the certificate application include an
Environmental Report, consisting of up to 13 Resource Reports as described in 18 CFR §§ 157.14(a)(6-a),
380.3, and 380.12. Each Resource Report describes a particular aspect of the environment and evaluates
the potential effects of the Project on the identified aspect. Resource Report 1 provides an overview of the
Project, including its purpose and need, a description of the proposed facilities, and associated land
requirements. The Resource Report also addresses procedures for construction, restoration, operation, and
maintenance of facilities, as well as required environmental permits and clearances. Additionally, it covers
non-jurisdictional facilities, future plans and abandonment, and cumulative impacts.

1.2     PURPOSE AND NEED

The Project’s purpose is to provide firm transportation service of up to 2.3 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d)
of natural gas from the Permian Basin to delivery points serving customers in New Mexico and Arizona
and to upgrade Transwestern’s existing Phoenix Lateral to allow bi-directional flow. The Project will serve
the need for additional natural gas supply in these states, driven by an increasing demand for (a) reliable
natural gas-powered electric generation and (b) natural gas deliveries via Local Distribution Companies. In
both cases, the natural gas is needed to serve the expanding population and industrial growth throughout
the Southwest. The Phoenix Lateral upgrades will support this expansion by adding the flexibility to
transport natural gas in both directions based on the operational needs of the integrated existing and
expansion pipeline facilities. The bi-directional flow capability will enable Transwestern to connect diverse
supply sources with delivery points to provide customers with access to a broader range of markets. This
flexibility strengthens the reliability and resilience of the overall Transwestern system by allowing
Transwestern to reroute gas supply in response to shifting demand patterns, supply constraints, and peak-
period conditions. This enhanced operational flexibility will also foster commodity price competition and
reduce price volatility for natural gas end users.

Transwestern has executed long-term, binding precedent agreements with Arizona Public Service Company
(APS), Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, Inc., Salt River Project Agricultural Improvement and Power
District (SRP), Southwest Gas Corporation, Tucson Electric Power Company (TEP), UNS Electric, Inc.,
New Mexico Gas Company (NMGC), and ETC Marketing Ltd., for a total of approximately 1.75 Bcf/d of
firm transportation service, representing approximately 76 percent of the Project’s total capacity. To meet
the customers’ gas supply needs, the Project’s target in-service date is June 2029. Transwestern expects
that growing demand in the project area will result in the remaining 0.55 Bcf/d of Project capacity being
fully subscribed. The execution of these binding commitments demonstrates that there is a clear market
demand for the capacity the Project is designed to provide and confirms that the proposed facilities are
necessary to ensure reliable natural gas delivery to the markets the Project will serve across New Mexico
and Arizona. Currently, of the Project’s approximate 1.75 Bcf/d firm transportation service, approximately
0.45 Bcf/d would be delivered to customers in New Mexico, with the remaining volume delivered to
Arizona customers.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Arizona’s total retail electricity sales
increased from 76.3 million megawatt-hours (MWh) in 2014 to 90.8 million MWh in 2024, (EIA 2014 and
2024), an increase of 19.1 percent. The increase was driven by rapid population growth and industrial
expansion. Major utilities broke peak usage records during the 2025 summer heat waves. EIA projections
forecast continued acceleration through 2026, consistent with a nationwide trend toward record-high
consumption. Arizona’s major electric companies (APS, SRP, and TEP – all Project customers) forecast
substantial continued growth. According to their 2025 FERC Form 714 submissions, the three utilities
project a combined non-coincident peak demand increase of approximately 35 percent by 2031 and 50
percent by 2034 relative to 2025 actual levels. The New Mexico Energy, Minerals, and Natural Resources
Department forecasted New Mexico utility total electricity demand will increase 42 percent from 2023 to
2040 (EMNRD 2024). This is not projected or modeled demand divorced from current conditions.
Similarly, New Mexico utilities expect electricity demand to grow by 42 percent over the next 14 years.
These growth projections, compounded by increased electrification of the economy and demand from
industrial expansion, drive the need for new infrastructure, including the Project.

In 2024, the Permian Basin reached a significant milestone, with marketed natural gas production averaging
25.4 Bcf/d, a 12 percent increase (roughly 2.7 Bcf/d) over 2023 levels, solidifying the basin’s role as the
primary engine for natural gas growth in the U.S. The Permian Basin alone now accounts for nearly a
quarter of all natural gas produced in the Lower 48 states. It is anticipated that the Permian Basin’s
production will grow to near 30 Bcf/d by 2030 based on EIA modeling. Accordingly, Transwestern’s
existing system, as expanded by the Project, is ideally positioned to transport the quantities of natural gas
required by Project customers from the Permian Basin to New Mexico and Arizona. The Project design
provides for access to Permian Basin receipt points, including construction of additional receipt laterals and
meters in Texas, that will flow gas to delivery points served by the Project’s delivery laterals and meters in
New Mexico and Arizona. These delivery laterals and meters originate from both the expansion and existing
pipeline facilities and terminate at various delivery points, including interconnections with El Paso Natural
Gas Company, LLC (EPNG).

cultural, paleontological, geological) surveys have been completed along the mainline and laterals. More
than 84 percent of the mainline has been surveyed for environmental resources (i.e., biological and cultural).
Environmental surveys for the laterals within Texas and New Mexico are between 95 and 100 percent
complete, and survey status for the Arizona laterals varies, with some nearing completion and some
beginning.

permanent easements (see typical right-of-way configuration figures in Appendix 1F).

        Bass Canyon would be completed by a dry open cut method (i.e., flume or dam and pump) to maintain flow

        Mojave Energy Park Lateral (10-inch). This 1.77-mile lateral takes off from Transwestern’s existing

        1.3.3     Aboveground Facilities
        1.3.3.1      Compressor Stations
        To meet the Project’s required contract pressures at the interconnects, compression will be added at the
        existing station at the beginning of the mainline (CS1-WT2), and eight new compressor stations will be
        constructed across the three states (see Table 1.3-3). Additionally, one other existing Transwestern
        compressor station (CS10-New River) will require compressor modifications to improve hydraulic
        performance, and piping systems will be modified to allow bidirectional gas flow on the existing
        Transwestern system. The proposed new compressor stations will be graveled and secured with a 7-foot-
        high chain-link fence topped with 1 foot of barbed wire.

        The new compressor units will be installed in new enclosures. Each unit will come equipped with Solar-
        provided auxiliary equipment, including a lube oil cooler, inlet air silencer/cleaner (huff n’ puff system),
        and exhaust system. Other equipment to be installed with each new compressor station will include: inlet
        filter separators, gas aftercoolers, turbine fuel gas conditioning skids, turbine fuel gas heaters, unit
        blowdown silencers, station piping blowdown silencers, seal gas racks, sump tanks, condensate storage
        tanks, and oily water storage tanks. The ancillary equipment at each new compressor station will include
        a skid-mounted air compressor enclosure and a back-up generator. Each generator will have dedicated fuel
        gas regulation and metering skids. A new Power Control Room building will also be installed at the site of
        each new compressor station to house critical electrical equipment. Related suction and discharge piping
        headers will be installed between the pipeline and each of the compressor units.

        New office/warehouse buildings will also be built within each new compressor station yard with phone and
        computer access. The facilities will not be manned 24 hours per day but will have emergency spare parts,
        portable equipment, and small hand tools stored on site. The facilities will be equipped with outside lighting
        for night work activities; however, these lights will only be utilized when the stations are manned. During
        operations, work or maintenance activities will not generally be scheduled at night; therefore, these lights
        will only be used periodically, if needed, for limited periods during the winter when daylight hours are
        shorter. Light fixtures will be shrouded to direct light down to station facilities.

        Compressor station locations are depicted on the maps in Appendix 1A-1, the alignment sheets in Appendix
        1B-1, and the maps in Appendix 1D-1. Plot plans, filed as CEII, are provided in Appendix 1C-1.

        Resource Report 9 addresses potential air quality and noise impacts associated with the new compressor
        stations.

        1.3.3.2        Meter Stations (Receipt and Delivery)
        Meter stations will be installed to facilitate the custody transfer of natural gas between interconnected
        parties and to control the flow rate of natural gas. Each meter station may include the following
        components: filtration, measurement, flow control, gas quality analyzer, remote actuation valves, telemetry
        and communications equipment, emergency backup power, isolation valves, security fencing, access
        roadways, and yard lighting. Some equipment will be housed in small buildings or under a weather shelter.
        Meter stations will vary in size to accommodate necessary equipment and maintenance activities (see Table
        1.3-4). The facility lights will only be utilized periodically when the stations are manned. During
        operations, work or maintenance activities will not generally be scheduled at night; therefore, these lights
        will only be used periodically, if needed, for limited periods during the winter when daylight hours are
        shorter. Light fixtures will be shrouded to direct light down to station facilities.

        The Project requires five (5) receipt meter stations to deliver gas to the mainline and 18 delivery meter
        stations to supply gas to customers. All receipt meter stations are located in Texas at the beginning of the
        receipt laterals and at the gas plant delivery points (see Table 1.3-4). The delivery meter stations will be
        located either along the mainline or at the end of the laterals at customer delivery points (see Table 1.3-4).

        The Project also requires two (2) regulator stations. The East Valley Regulator, located at the end of the
        mainline (MP 525.1), will expand Transwestern’s existing 3.2-acre East Valley Meter Station by 8.4 acres.
        This station will include a 48-inch receiver, a regulator facility1, a tie-in between Transwestern’s existing
        36-inch pipeline and the Germann Lateral’s launcher, and a tie-in to the 48-inch mainline. The second
        regulator station (Ash Fork) will be located within Transwestern’s existing aboveground facility near Ash
        Fork in Yavapai County, Arizona. Modifications within the facility will require no new disturbance and
        will allow bi-directional gas flow.

        Meter and regulator station locations are depicted on the maps in Appendix 1A-1 and Appendix 1A-2, on
        the alignment sheets in Appendix 1B-1 and Appendix 1B-2, and on the maps in Appendix 1D-1. Plot plans,
        filed as CEII, are provided in Appendix 1C-2.

        1.3.3.3        Valves – Mainline
        Mainline valves (MLVs or valves) will be located along the mainline in accordance with U.S. Department
        of Transportation’s (DOT’s) Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) spacing
        requirements (49 CFR § 192.179). MLVs will be automated and remotely operated with natural gas over
        hydraulic actuators powered by a solar and battery system. Each MLV will occupy an 80 feet x 60 feet
        (0.11-acre) site and will be centered on the pipeline within the proposed permanent easement. The MLVs
        will have a gravel or caliche finished grade and will be enclosed within a 7-foot-high chain-link security
        fence or co-located with an existing fenced launcher/receiver or compressor station. The Project has
        attempted to locate the valves adjacent to existing roads to minimize the length of new permanent access

        1.4.1.1       Construction Right-of-Way
        Temporary Construction Right-of-Way. Transwestern has designed a typical 150-foot-wide temporary
        construction right-of-way for the 48-inch diameter mainline. The construction right-of-way configuration
        is required to accommodate the necessary clearing and grading activities for preparation of the right-of-way
        for safe construction, to temporarily store spoil from grading and trenching operations, and to string and
        fabricate the pipe materials. The proposed right-of-way configuration also considers the size of equipment
        necessary to safely handle and fabricate the 48-inch pipe materials and the various operations during
        construction. Additionally, it provides a bi-directional travel lane, which is necessary for equipment
        moving up and down the right-of-way to expedite construction, especially given the remoteness along
        certain segments of the right-of-way. The temporary construction right-of-way will be used as the primary
        transportation corridor during construction. Narrowing the right-of-way width and eliminating the travel
        lane would significantly restrict traffic flow along the right-of-way, and efficient traffic flow minimizes
        impacts by reducing the number of access roads that may need to be constructed and by minimizing
        construction duration. The construction right-of-way width also accommodates the various changes in soil
        and topographic conditions across the Project. Appendix 1E provides a detailed justification for the 150-
        foot-width request based on the equipment needed to install large-diameter pipe, trench depth and width,
        and other parameters.

        The proposed typical construction right-of-way widths for the lateral pipelines are:

            •     75 feet for the 6-, 10-, 16-, and 20-inch laterals
            •     90 feet for the 24- and 30-inch laterals
        Appendix 1F provides the typical construction right-of-way figures. Based on site-specific conditions, the
        construction right-of-way widths for the mainline and laterals may vary.
        Additional Temporary Workspace (ATWS). In addition to the construction right-of-way, site-specific
        conditions require ATWS. The ATWS may be required for (but not limited to) the following:
            •     road, pipeline, railroad and canal crossings for bore pits, spoil storage, staging and parking;
            •     sharp angles or points of intersection (PIs) where additional area is required for pipe bending,
                  fittings and to account for the wide turning radius and turn arounds for stringing trucks (which can
                  be greater than 100 feet in length);
            •     spoil storage, staging, residential and industrial areas, etc.;
            •     steep slopes and side sloping areas to accommodate cuts and spoil storage requirements;
            •     pipe, material, equipment staging and parking;
            •     areas where tie-ins require additional trench widths to allow workers to enter the trench and perform
                  welds and to ensure Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) trench safety
                  requirements are met; and
            •     topsoil segregation areas to ensure topsoil and subsoils are not mixed in agricultural areas.

        Road and other tie-in locations are typically conducted with a separate construction crew to fabricate and
        install the pipeline across these features. To conduct these crossings, ATWS is required to stage or
        accommodate the equipment, crew vehicles, pipeline materials, dig the trench, store the spoil and safely
        install the pipeline.

        ATWS are considered temporary disturbance and will be reclaimed upon completion of construction (see
        Erosion Control and Revegetation Plan [ECRP] in Appendix 1G).

        FERC’s Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures (FERC’s Procedures) contain
        specifications regarding the location of ATWS in proximity to waterbodies and wetlands. As described in

        Resource Report 2, survey efforts in Texas delineated only two emergent wetlands, and they are associated
        with the two surveyed perennial waterbodies in Texas, the Pecos River at MP 31.33 and Salt Creek at MP
        43.74; the perennial waterbodies and associated wetlands will be crossed and avoided by HDD. No
        wetlands were delineated in New Mexico or Arizona. No perennial waterbodies were surveyed in New
        Mexico. Surveys in Arizona delineated the Central Arizona Project (CAP) and Pima canals in Arizona;
        these are man-made features with artificial perennial flow. The CAP and Pima canals will also be crossed
        by HDD. Field surveys delineated ephemeral and intermittent features (mostly dry washes), ditches, and
        canals along the mainline and laterals. Transwestern has identified measures in FERC’s Procedures that
        are considered unnecessary, technically infeasible, or unsuitable because of the Project’s location in the
        desert regions of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona and has described alternatives applicable to the desert
        environment (see Appendix 1G).

        As defined in FERC’s Procedures (I.B.1), waterbodies are any natural or artificial stream, river, or drainage
        with perceptible flow at the time of crossing, and other permanent waterbodies such as ponds and lakes.
        FERC’s Procedures (V.B.2.a.) require all extra work areas (such as staging areas and additional spoil
        storage areas) to be located at least 50 feet away from water’s edge, except where the adjacent upland
        consists of cultivated or rotated cropland or other disturbed land. Transwestern has located all ATWS at
        least 50 feet from waterbody boundaries (intermittent and ephemeral dry washes), where feasible, based on
        topographic conditions or other existing constraints. FERC’s Procedures (V.B.3.g.) allow waterbodies to
        be crossed using standard upland construction techniques when they are dry and not flowing, provided that
        the Environmental Inspector (EI) verifies that water is unlikely to flow between initial disturbance and final
        stabilization of the feature.

        During construction at dry wash (includes ephemeral and intermittent) crossings, where approved by the EI
        and Chief Inspector, Transwestern may shift the ATWS to be within 10 feet of the top bank when no water
        is present. These ATWS shifts would occur within the existing biological and cultural survey corridor, and
        the EI would ensure that no cultural or biological resources would be affected by the ATWS shifts and that
        landowner permission has been obtained. When no water is present, the shifts would minimize equipment,
        emissions, and the time required to push/move spoil materials back 50 feet from the dry wash crossings and
        to return the spoil material during trench backfilling and bank regrading and stabilization. The desert habitat
        communities adjacent to many of these dry wash crossings are similar to the adjacent uplands and lack
        perceptible differences in vegetation species composition and densities. The EI would ensure appropriate
        erosion control Best Management Practices (BMPs) are installed to prevent spoil and sediment from
        entering the dry washes from adjacent upland areas.

        1.4.1.2      Permanent Easement
        A permanent easement is needed for long-term operation and maintenance of the mainline and laterals. The
        width of the permanent easement for the mainline on all lands will be 60 feet, centered over the pipe as
        installed or, depending on the location, may be offset 40 feet x 20 feet. The permanent easement widths
        for the laterals will vary based on diameter, with 6-, 10-, 16-, and 20-inch diameter laterals having a 30-
        foot permanent easement and 24- and 30-inch diameter laterals having a 50-foot permanent easement. For
        the 48-inch diameter mainline, a 60-foot, rather than a 50-foot, permanent easement is necessary for
        maintenance activities to allow for sufficient space to meet OSHA trenching excavation safety
        requirements. Appendix 1E provides a detailed justification for the 60-foot-width request.

        Transwestern will negotiate perpetual easements for the mainline and lateral permanent easements. There
        will be a one-time payment to private landowners based on, for example, the impact of the easements on
        the properties (i.e., impact of the easements on the functional utility of the land). The easements will restrict
        placement of permanent structures. Subject to Transwestern’s safety, maintenance, and operational
        requirements, the easements may be crossed by roads, fences, utilities, etc. The easements will include one

        Existing egress and ingress points to and from the construction rights-of-way for the mainline and laterals

        In some areas, it may be necessary to grade or widen a limited number of existing roads at select locations
        to accommodate large equipment, such as lowboys and pipe stringing trucks, to provide appropriate turning
        radius, and allow two-way traffic for access to the construction right-of-way. The stringing trucks will be
        hauling approximately 80-foot joints of pipe. The total length of these vehicles may be more than 100 feet
        and therefore these vehicles may require a modified road footprint, especially on corners and with oncoming
        traffic. Widening and grading access roads in the identified constricted locations is also necessary to
        accommodate the potential for the stringing trucks to “travel” outside of the existing road footprint as well
        as maintain span clearance between axles. In some circumstances, it may also be necessary for oncoming
        traffic to “pull out” of the existing road footprint for passing purposes.

        Minor improvements (e.g., limbing, potholing and grading to remove ruts and surfacing) may be needed in
        some areas to accommodate construction equipment. In general, roadway improvements will require a
        minimal amount of site disturbance and earthwork necessary to make the roads useable for access to the
        construction right-of-way. All maintenance will conform to applicable federal, state, and local
        requirements as well as landowner stipulations included in easement agreements. No maintenance or
        improvements will be allowed on any road not authorized for use and approved for improvements.

        Temporary Access Roads. Transwestern has identified existing roads that will be used for temporary
        construction access (see Table 8A-1 and Table 8A-2 in Appendix 8A to Resource Report 8). If necessary
        to facilitate construction, road improvements outside the existing road prism may include maintenance
        grading and surfacing, curve widening, traffic turnouts, or widening for two-way traffic. Environmental
        and cultural surveys are on-going for the temporary access roads where permission has been obtained and
        results will be provided in future submittals Road improvements will remain after construction unless
        otherwise stipulated in landowner agreements. Temporary access roads will be maintained throughout
        construction and will be left in preconstruction conditions or better.

        New Temporary Access Roads. Transwestern may identify locations where it will be necessary to
        construct new temporary access roads (N-TAR); if N-TAR’s are needed, they will be provided in the FERC
        certificate application. The status of these roads following completion of construction will be as stipulated

        hydro ax, or a bulldozer. This material will be salvaged on the edge of the construction right-of-way,
        incorporated into the top 6 inches or less of rangeland surface soil and then redistributed or scattered across
        the right-of-way after seeding during final cleanup (see Transwestern’s FERC Plan in Appendix 1G).
        Hayfields and vegetation types, such as grasslands, low shrubs, or other low-growth vegetation, will not be
        cleared except in areas directly over the trench or where topsoil salvage or grading will be required. The
        cleared vegetation material will be incorporated into the topsoil or stored on the edge of the right-of-way
        and spread back over disturbed areas during final restoration. This material will increase moisture retention
        and reduce wind and water erosion and will provide an important source of native seed and vegetive
        propagules; it can be considered equivalent to mulch, depending on the quantity of vegetative/mulch cover.
        In Arizona, Transwestern will appropriately permit and conduct land clearing requirements according to
        the Arizona Department of Agriculture Native Plants Administrative Code rules (see Article 11). Clearing
        and grading activities will also follow the procedures outlined in the noxious weed control section in the
        ECRP (see Appendix 1G).

        1.5.1.2.7   Topsoiling
        Transwestern’s FERC Plan (Section IV.B.1) requires topsoil segregation in: 1) all residential areas; 2)
        annually cultivated or rotated agricultural lands and pasture; 3) hayfields; and 4) other areas at the
        landowner’s request. In these areas, Transwestern’s FERC Plan requires either full work area or trench line
        and subsoil storage area stripping.

        As outlined in Transwestern’s FERC Plan (IV.B.1.7), in rangelands, 6 inches or less of the soil surface or
        desert pavement, that can be feasibly salvaged from the trench line and working side of the construction
        right-of-way, will be salvaged together with the cleared vegetative material. The vegetative material will
        be removed by mowing, mulching, or scalping off the tops of the shrubs with a brush hog, hydro ax, or a
        bulldozer. The salvaged material will provide a source of seed and vegetative propagules (i.e., roots,
        rhizomes, solons, etc.) to improve revegetation success. The surface soil, desert pavement, and cleared
        vegetation material will be left in-place on the non-working (or topographically appropriate) side of the
        right-of-way (topsoil and spoil storage areas), where the mowed/mulched vegetation material will provide
        a vegetative/organic marker for operators during backfilling and regrading operations. It will indicate that
        they have reached the original ground surface during backfilling and topsoil spreading operations to
        minimize disturbance to the undisturbed soils on the non-working side of the right-of-way. The EI, Chief
        Inspector, or Transwestern representative will determine areas where it is not feasible to salvage rangeland
        topsoil based on topographic conditions, available workspace, and bedrock or surface rock conditions. The
        vegetation and topsoil materials may be salvaged on either side or both sides and within the construction
        right-of-way, to minimize movement of topsoil during grading and restoration activities as determined
        during construction. Where it is not feasible to salvage rangeland topsoil, Transwestern will report the
        locations by MP and provide the rationale to FERC in weekly or bi-weekly reports.

        To minimize disturbance to desert rangelands, Transwestern proposes to store the salvaged vegetative and
        surface soils materials within the construction right-of-way rather than proposing additional ATWS to store
        the material. In rugged topographic areas, excavated spoil material may be placed abutting and potentially
        on top of the salvaged vegetation/surface soils to minimize the need for ATWS. The grading/
        excavating/restoring sequence will be a first out/last in approach. This means the soil first excavated will
        be the last material redistributed across the right-of-way to preserve the topsoil/soil seed bank. It is
        Transwestern’s opinion that creating additional disturbance (i.e., ATWS) in desert habitats to separate the
        salvaged surface materials from the spoil is not beneficial and would create more long-term disturbance
        impacts.

        1.5.1.2.9   Trenching
        The depth of the trench will be sufficient to provide a minimum depth of cover of 30 inches in normal soil,
        18 inches in consolidated rock, and at least 48 inches in agriculture lands. Transwestern will strive to
        exceed these minimum DOT requirements provided in 49 CFR Part 192 where feasible and will achieve 36
        inches of cover in Class I locations with normal soils and up to 24 inches of cover in consolidated rock
        areas.

        For Class II, III, and IV locations, as well as drainage ditches of paved county, city, and state road and
        railroad crossings, DOT regulations provided in 49 CFR Part 192 require a minimum cover of 36 inches in
        normal soil and 24 inches in consolidated rock.

        1.5.1.2.10 Pipe Installation
        After trenching is completed, the pipe sections will be strung along the trench, bent to fit the contour of the
        trench bottom, aligned, welded together, and placed on temporary supports along the edge of the trench.
        All welds will be visually inspected, non-destructively tested (using radiographic or equivalent methods),
        and repaired, if necessary. Line pipe, normally mill-coated prior to stringing, will require field applied
        coating at the welded joints prior to final inspection. The entire pipeline coating will be inspected and
        tested to locate and repair any flaws or voids. The pipe assembly will then be lowered into the trench by
        side-boom tractors and excavators.

        On the mainline, Transwestern has identified locations where HDDs will be utilized to cross
        environmentally sensitive areas or major highways and railroads, where additional burial depth may be
        required (see Table 1.5-3). Transwestern may replace proposed HDD crossings with other trenchless
        methods. To facilitate the HDD crossings, ATWS will be required at the entry and exit points; the ATWS
        is typically 350 feet x 300 feet to stage the drill rig, ancillary equipment, machinery and materials and
        complete the drill. For some HDDs, an ATWS will be required to accommodate the HDD pullback string
        assembly at the HDD exit so that the entire pullback string can be fabricated in one section, which will
        allow the HDD pullback process to be completed without stopping to weld on additional pipe sections.
        Stopping the pullback process increases the potential for the pipeline section to become lodged. There is
        not enough space at Rio Grande River/RR HDD to accommodate the entire pullback string assembly in a
        single section. A middle weld will be required during the pullback.

        During the Project’s final design phase, Transwestern will determine the number of test sections which will
        have varying lengths and water volume requirements (see Table 1.5-6). During the test, it may be necessary
        to release water at each of the section breaks; however, Transwestern will conserve water as much as
        practical and minimize release by cascading water between test sections, where feasible. Additionally,
        where feasible, water that does need to be released may be stored in tanks or lined ponds and used for dust
        control or hydroseeding. Without cascading, the maximum test volume for all individual test segments
        would be approximately 805 acre-feet (262 million gallons). With the use of cascading, the minimum test
        water volume is estimated to be approximately 300-acre feet (98 million gallons). The actual volume will
        be within this range and is expected to be at the lower end of the range.

        Permission to release the hydrostatic test water will be obtained through the governing agencies. Release
        rates would range from several hundred gallons per minute (gpm) to several thousand gpm. The specific
        hydrostatic release rate at each dewater location cannot be estimated at this time because the rate will be
        dependent on contractor means and methods plus a number of factors specific to each location. These
        variables include: the volume of water to be released, completion dates for adjoining test segments,
        topographic conditions of the location, elevation differences between test sections and the direction of flow
        (uphill/downhill) between the test section, size of the test head piping, kind and size of the dewater structure,
        infiltration properties of the surrounding soils, and location of any sensitive resources such as wetlands and
        waterbodies or facilities (e.g., roads, residences) in the vicinity of the dewater location. The rate would be
        controlled to prevent scour, erosion, and potential effects or sediment migration to sensitive resources or
        facilities (see ECRP in Appendix 1G).

        Water sourcing and disposal associated with hydrostatic testing of the compressor stations will be the
        responsibility of the contractors building the facilities. They will supply and dispose of water used.

        1.5.1.2.13 Cleanup and Permanent Erosion Control Devices
        Transwestern will endeavor to complete final cleanup of an area within 35 days after backfilling the trench,
        where practicable. Final cleanup will include final grading and installation of permanent erosion control
        structures. In no case will Transwestern delay final cleanup beyond the end of the next recommended
        seeding season. During rough cleanup, Transwestern will remove all construction debris and grade
        disturbed areas to approximate preconstruction grade to the extent practicable. Transwestern anticipates
        completing final cleanup during fall and winter of 2029 and 2030 unless active travel lanes remain open
        along specific locations of the right-of-way where access may be required for out-of-sequence final
        restoration activities.

        Travel Lane. Because of the restricted nature of the construction right-of-way in several areas,
        Transwestern anticipates that it will be necessary to leave a travel lane open over extended portions of the
        construction right-of-way. Once access is no longer required, the travel lane will be closed and the disturbed
        area reclaimed. To reduce erosion from the travel lane, Transwestern will install appropriate temporary
        erosion controls in areas where the travel lane is temporarily left open. These are discussed in the project-
        specific ECRP provided in Appendix 1G.

        Excess Rock Removal. Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Section V.A.3) requires the removal of excess
        rock from the top 12 inches of soil in cultivated or rotated croplands, hayfields, pastures, residential areas,
